name: Ochre Yellow
lede: Ochre Yellow is the pale golden yellow that Werner's nineteenth-century color chart matched to a bird's feathers and a polished stone, named for yellow ochre, the iron-rich earth that painters have dug for pigment since the Palaeolithic.

sections.title: A pale yellow with a brown name
sections.body:
Greek was already loose about the idea. The prefix *ochro-* is Greek for pale yellow, and *okros* is one of the Greek words for yellow, beside *xanthos*, *chloros*, *chrysos*, *melinos* and *krokinos*, and Pastoureau notes that such words convey effects of light or saturation more than a fixed material hue [5]. Latin had *silaceus* for ochre yellow among its rarer yellow words [5].

English dictionaries do not settle it either. Paterson glosses *ochre yellow* as a yellowish brown and *ochreous* as a light yellowy brown, while his entry for *ochro-* says pale yellow [3]. St Clair gives ocher as a pale yellowish brown [4]. The word therefore runs from pale yellow to brown, and the swatch on this page sits at the pale, golden end [3][4][15].

The phrase *ochre yellow* is a naturalist's term as much as a painter's. It is one of the colors in Werner's mineral nomenclature of 1774, and Patrick Syme's chart gave it a painted swatch and examples from birds and stones [1][2].

sections.title: Number 74
sections.body:
Werner's first list of 1774 contained 54 colors, and ochre yellow was one of its nine yellows, beside sulphur, lemon, straw, wine and Isabella yellow [1]. Baty's chart shows it again in later lists, among them Lenz, Widenmann, Kirwan and Picardet [1].

In Syme's chart it is number 74, marked with a W as one of Werner's own [2]. His recipe is sienna yellow with a little light chesnut brown, while sienna yellow itself, number 73, is primrose yellow with a little ochre yellow [2]. The two recipes lean on each other, and on screen the two swatches sit only 1.7 units apart [15].

Ochre yellow was also a building block. Syme made straw yellow from sulphur yellow, much greyish white and a little ochre yellow, and cream yellow from ochre yellow with some white and the merest trace of Dutch orange [2]. Cream yellow was his new name for Werner's Isabella yellow [2]. His examples for number 74 were the vent coverts of the redstart, which are the feathers around the cloaca, and porcelain jasper [2].

sections.title: The earth behind the name
sections.body:
The pigment is yellow ochre, an earth colored mainly by goethite, a hydrated iron oxide [6]. Geologists call such soft, fine-grained deposits limonites [6]. Yellow ochres form in all climates, but goethite-rich soils are most typical of higher-latitude, humid places where the ground rarely dries out [6].

Preparation is simple. The earth is washed, levigated and ground, and the result is a very stable pigment that works in every medium [6]. Fire changes it: burnt, yellow ochre goes brown, red and violet as the goethite turns to iron(III) oxide, a technology that seems to have been available since the Palaeolithic [6].

A true ochre carries no manganese, which separates it from [[sienna]] and [[umber]] [7]. The Compendium notes that siennas are often called a variety of yellow ochre, but they contain small amounts of manganese oxide [6]. A rarer iron mineral, lepidocrocite, sometimes joins goethite in yellow ochre soils, and its name is Greek for a saffron-colored flake [6][8].

Because it was cheap, ochre was cut with other things. Church recorded in 1901 that yellow ochre could be adulterated with turmeric or other organic yellows, or with chrome yellow, and Dossie suggested Dutch pink as an additive as early as 1764 [6].

sections.title: From cave walls to Roman villas
sections.body:
Yellow ochre is among the earliest pigments. It has been identified in European Palaeolithic cave art, though it was used far less than red ochre or burnt ochre, and in the rock art of more recent Aboriginal cultures [6]. Egyptian painters used it, sometimes adulterated with orpiment, and occasionally mixed it with blue frit to make green [6][12]. It also appears in wall paintings and reliefs from Persepolis and in Roman wall paintings [6].

The most celebrated yellow ochre of antiquity came from the silver mines at Laurion, west of Athens, and was known as Attic ochre [6]. By Vitruvius' account in the first century BC its supply was exhausted, yet Pliny, writing in AD 77, still quotes two denarii a pound for it, which the Compendium calls confusing [6]. Vitruvius calls yellow ochre *ochra* and *sil*, Pliny calls it *sil*, and between them they name sources in Italy, Scyros, Gaul, Rome, Lydia and Achaia [6].

Pliny is also the source of a story that the great Greek painters, Apelles among them, used only four colors: Melian white, Attic ochre yellow, Pontic red and black [10]. That is a myth. Pliny was moralising against luxury, and Greek painters did use blues such as Egyptian blue [10]. Ochre belongs to the plain, sober end of the ancient palette, but it was never the whole of it.

sections.title: On the palette
sections.body:
Yellow ochre is a staple of Byzantine and medieval art, especially icons and frescoes [6]. The Compendium traces it in Signorelli's panel paintings, in a portrait miniature of Elizabeth I, on the palettes of Vermeer, Turner, van Goyen and van Ruysdael, and in Mexican devotional painting [6]. The Italian painter Cennino Cennini recommended ochre above all for hair and drapery, and mixed verdaccio, his color for mountains, from one part black and two parts ochre [11].

A few painters leaned on it for color they would not buy. Velázquez never used a pure green, and mixed his greens from azurite with yellow ochre or lead-tin yellow [12]. In the twentieth century, Le Corbusier and Ozenfant put ochre yellows beside reds, earths, white, black and ultramarine in the stable "major scale" of Purism, colors they called strong and constructive and said had served in all the great periods [14].

To find the pale end of the family, look for ochre thinned with white: Syme's cream yellow is exactly that [2].

sections.title: Oxford, Bristol, Périgord
sections.body:
Ochre was dug locally and named for the place. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the Oxford area, on Jurassic ironstone, produced what was thought the best yellow ochre in Britain [7]. John Smith's *Art of Painting* of 1676 says most of the yellow ochre sold in England was dug on the Shotover Hills near Oxford, and praises it for grinding fine, bearing a good body and resisting weather [6]. The name *Oxford ochre* only came in the nineteenth century [9]. Bristol was another source, and its good yellow ochre was also called Bristol yellow [7]. By 1928 Heaton reported that Shotover's supplies were almost exhausted [6].

French ochre was the bright yellow one. It came from the Périgord, the Yonne valley and the Vaucluse, and was sold in five grades, from common yellow (*jaune commun*) to an extra-superfine levigated deep yellow [6].

Books disagree about the color of Roman ochre [6][9]. By Harley's account, as the Compendium reports it, Italian or Roman ochre from southern Italy and Sicily was a warm, reddish yellow, while Salter in 1869 described Roman ochre as deeper and more transparent than ordinary yellow ochre, and cool in tint [6][9].

Names kept old guesses alive. *Ocre de rue* may have been taken by French writers for an English place name, though Mérimée suggested that *ru* meant *ruisseau*, a riverside iron deposit [9]. Spruce ochre was apparently a corruption of Prussian ochre, named for a deposit [6]. A Winsor and Newton catalogue of 1896 listed gold ochre as an earth more powerful than Oxford ochre [18].

sections.title: Which yellow is it?
sections.body:
The swatch here is Syme's number 74 as scanned from an aged chart, #EFCC83, a light warm gold [15]. It is much lighter than a lump of the earth. RAL, the German industrial color standard, lists an ochre yellow as RAL 1024, about #BA8F4C on screen, which is 16.5 CIEDE2000 units darker and duller [15].

The family color [[ochre]], #CC7722, is a strong orange 24.4 units away [15]. The dictionary's yellowish brown, [[yellowish-brown]], is 30.7 units away [15]. Nearer neighbors are [[beige]] at 8.9 units and the near-twin Sienna Yellow at 1.7 [15]. The nearest ISCC-NBS block calls this swatch a light orange yellow, 4.0 units away [15].

So three things share the name: a pale gold in Werner's chart, a mid-tone gold-brown in the RAL system, and a range of yellowish browns in dictionaries [3][15]. They are neighbors, not duplicates.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six CIEDE2000 units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 399 works, about 1.7 per cent [16]. Inside those pictures it is almost always one of the lightest tones, in 99 per cent of the matches, as a pale color should be [16].

The largest areas are in East Asian and Indian pictures [16]. [[painting:aic-92961|Bamboo]] by Kishi Ganku (1801) has three-quarters of its surface inside the threshold, and Yun Shouping's [[painting:cma-143237|Herbaceous Peony]] (1685) is close behind [16]. Japanese paintings carry the color in 32 of 698 works, 2.7 times the archive rate, and the Kalighat bazaar paintings of Calcutta in 12 of 96, 7.5 times [16]. In ink-and-color works the aged silk or paper ground can read as this color by itself, so the match is not always pigment [16].

By decade the highest rate is the 1820s, with 31 of 731 paintings, 2.5 times the archive rate [16]. Among painters with enough works, [[painter:jan-both|Jan Both]] has it in 3 of 18, [[painter:thomas-sully|Thomas Sully]] in 3 of 25 and [[painter:pierre-bonnard|Bonnard]] in 3 of 45, while [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]] has the most, 6 of 287 [16]. The earliest dated match is a Virgin and Child of 1305 at about 20 per cent of its surface [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [16].

In Google Books the phrase *ochre yellow* peaks in the 1810s, the decade of Syme's first edition, and by the 2000s it stands near 7 per cent of that peak [17].
